papers.title: Dissociation of Reward Incentive and Motivational Drive by Distinct Neural Circuits in Mice
papers.abstract: The generation of reward incentive value and maintenance of motivational drive are distinct processes in reward-related behavior. However, how neural circuits differentially process these components remains poorly understood. Although intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS) paradigms have been utilized to identify reward-related circuits, ICSS measures may conflate reinitiated actions attributed to learned incentive value with ongoing motivated behavior sustained by concurrent stimulation. Here, we reveal a dissociation between these processes by optogenetically stimulating fibers in the stria terminalis bundle projecting to the medial nucleus accumbens (STBmNAc) and those in the medial forebrain bundle originating from the lateral NAc (MFBlNAc). We found that STBmNAc stimulation facilitated the reinitiation of ICSS actions, whereas MFBlNAc stimulation sustained ongoing ICSS behavior. Moreover, shortening the stimulation duration in STBmNAc mice increased the likelihood of subsequent re-engagement of stimulation-seeking. Additionally, STBmNAc stimulation, but not MFBlNAc stimulation, could substitute for primary rewards and support the acquisition of sensory cue-dependent operant behavior. Together, our findings suggest that STBmNAc activation promotes reward-anticipatory behavior by conferring reward incentive value, whereas MFBlNAc activation sustains ongoing behavior by maintaining motivational drive. Thus, reward-related behavior may not be governed by a unitary motivational system but may involve anatomically and functionally distinct neural components.

papers.title: Learning human-robot collaboration reshapes biological motor coordination
papers.abstract: Wearable augmentation robots expand human motor capabilities, but every added degree of freedom creates a new coordination problem for the biological body. Although previous studies have made substantial advances in robot sensing, control, and safety, they have largely overlooked how the users own movement changes: individuals adapt their body movements when they start using an augmentation robot, even when control does not require it, and this coordination pattern continues to change as they gain proficiency. Consequently, users may struggle to accommodate robot-related restructuring of their movements during prolonged use, potentially increasing the risk of user rejection or abandonment. Over five days of training, 26 participants performed tasks with a wearable robotic digit and a tool-use control task, allowing us to longitudinally characterise and compare body-wide movement patterns between the two. Performance improved similarly across tasks, but the underlying motor coordination trajectories diverged. During augmentation, biological finger and limb coordination departed progressively further from its initial structure than during tool use, and joints increasingly varied together in ways that kept task performance stable, indicating that a new, body-wide augmented motor pattern continued to develop across days. These findings demonstrate that the biological motor system is not a fixed substrate that can be simply augmented with artificial limbs, but rather its movement patterns continuously evolve as users learn to control an added effector. Characterising this evolving motor solution informs the design, training, and evaluation of augmentation systems, supporting the sustained integration of added effectors into the human motor system. One-Sentence SummaryRobots that work with the body face a moving target, as collaborating with one teaches people entirely new ways to move.

papers.title: PICALM deficiency exacerbates amyloid pathology in murine and nematode Alzheimers disease models
papers.abstract: Alzheimers disease (AD), characterized by the accumulation of amyloid {beta}-peptide (A{beta}) plaques, is a progressive age-related neurodegenerative disorder affecting more than 35 million people worldwide. The risk of developing AD is significantly influenced by genetic factors. Deciphering their molecular functions has substantially advanced our understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms underlying AD. The PICALM gene represents a highly validated AD risk factor, and the encoded endocytic adaptor CALM is critical for endothelial A{beta} clearance and microglial A{beta} phagocytosis. However, it remains controversial how neuronally expressed CALM modulates AD pathogenesis. We find that loss of neuronal CALM accelerates A{beta} plaque formation and impairs neurotransmission in an AD mouse model, revealing a protective role for neuronal CALM. These phenotypes are accompanied by an elevated surface level of the endolysosomal SNARE protein VAMP8, consistent with a role for CALM in promoting the turnover of aggregated proteins via the autophagy/lysosome pathway. Moreover, loss of CALM promotes A{beta} aggregation in a C. elegans model expressing fluorescently labelled A{beta}, while neuron-specific overexpression of CALM decreases A{beta} aggregation. Finally, we demonstrate that the ANTH domain of CALM displays chaperone-like activity by inhibiting A{beta} aggregation in vitro. Our combined data suggest that neuronal CALM might counteract AD progression by suppressing A{beta} aggregation and by safeguarding endolysosomal SNARE trafficking.

papers.title: Gaze and Pupil Patterns in ADHD and ASD during Naturalistic Viewing
papers.abstract: BackgroundAutism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occur, and both are associated with atypical attention and arousal. Whether these associations arise from shared or distinct processes remains unclear because the conditions are rarely modeled jointly and attention and arousal are rarely measured simultaneously. MethodsWe analyzed eye-tracking data (gaze position and pupil size) collected during naturalistic video viewing from 2,421 youth (aged 5-22) in the Healthy Brain Network. ASD, ADHD-Inattentive, and ADHD-Hyperactive diagnostic statuses were modeled jointly alongside age and sex. ResultsAtypical gaze trajectories were uniquely associated with ASD. Basic oculomotor control and orienting after scene cuts and to faces were typical, but autistic participants maintained gaze consistently farther from typical viewing locations and spent less time looking at characters, faces, and mouths. Pupil fluctuations were atypical in both ASD and ADHD-Hyperactivity via distinct routes: reduced pupil synchrony in ASD was largely explained by gaze allocation, whereas in ADHD-Hyperactivity it was gaze-independent and accompanied by faster pupil fluctuations. ConclusionsASD and ADHD show dissociable signatures during natural viewing: ASD differs in what is looked at rather than when, whereas ADHD-Hyperactivity is characterized by faster-fluctuating arousal.

papers.title: Aiolos is specifically altered in schizophrenia, is expressed in hippocampal neurons and regulates structural synaptic plasticity through complement-mediated mechanisms
papers.abstract: Aiolos (Ikzf3), a member of the Ikzf family, has been primarily characterized in the immune system, whereas other Ikzf family members have reported roles in the brain and have been implicated in schizophrenia. However, the potential role of Aiolos in the brain remains broadly unexplored. Combining human samples, translational and gain and loss of function mouse models we characterized Aiolos expression in the brain and investigated its potential involvement in schizophrenia. Here we show that Aiolos expression varies across brain regions and developmental stages, stabilizing in principal neurons during adulthood. Moreover, we identified that Aiolos is dysregulated in peripheral immune cells and in the hippocampus of patients with schizophrenia. Modeling the impact of those dysregulations in mice induced behavioral phenotypes relevant to the positive, negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia. Finally, we found that mimicking Aiolos hippocampal dysregulation in mice generated increased complement protein abundance, accompanied by microglia-associated loss of synaptic material. Our results suggest that Aiolos may regulate complement-mediated synaptic elimination with potential implications for schizophrenia.

papers.title: Optogenetic Kindling Model Reveals Functional Synaptopathy as a Driver of Temporal Lobe Epilepsy and Associated Comorbidities
papers.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is one of the most prevalent and pharmaco-resistant forms of focal epilepsy in adults. The precise cellular and network mechanisms underlying TLE progression remain elusive. Animal models are essential for studying molecular and cellular mechanisms of TLE; however, widely used models largely rely on acute seizure induction and fail to recapitulate the gradual, progressive course of human TLE. Here, we present an optogenetic kindling mouse model of TLE, in which repeated stimulation induces a progressive increase in seizure susceptibility. This mouse model exhibits prominent TLE phenotypes, including robust hippocampal epileptiform activity, behavioral seizures, emotional changes, reactive astrogliosis, and impaired hippocampal learning and memory. Moreover, hippocampal synaptic analyses of this model revealed altered synaptic transmission and plasticity, without structural changes in excitatory or inhibitory synapses or overt cell death. These findings demonstrate that progressive epileptogenesis, synaptic dysfunction and TLE-associated phenotypes can develop independently of structural remodeling or overt cell death. This model provides a platform for investigating the synaptic mechanisms underlying TLE-associated synaptopathy.

papers.title: Expression of human-specific SRGAP2C increases representational capacity in mice
papers.abstract: The brain of modern humans has evolved remarkable computational abilities enabling higher cognitive functions. Recent progress in evolutionary genomics and experimental neuroscience has identified several human-specific genetic modifiers of brain development that underlie the emergence of human-specific traits of cortical circuit connectivity and function. The human-specific gene SRGAP2C emerged by partial duplication of the ancestral gene SRGAP2A, which encodes a postsynaptic protein regulating synaptic development. SRGAP2C inhibits all known functions of SRGAP2A and its expression in mouse cortical pyramidal neurons leads to neotenic synaptic maturation, increased cortico-cortical connectivity, increased reliability of sensory coding by cortical layer 2/3 PNs, and improved learning of a sensory discrimination task. However, it remains unclear whether SRGAP2C expression in the mouse cortex is sufficient to produce changes in cognition. To test this idea, we trained adult wild-type (WT) and SRGAP2C mice on a Go-NoGo task that involves learning to associate a whisker stimulus with the presence of a water reward. SRGAP2C mice displayed a licking strategy that accelerated the learning of stimulus-reward associations at the cost of punishment timeouts compared to WT mice. The licking strategy was selective to the task, not driven by a general increase in consumptive behavior, and it accelerated the information that SRGAP2C mice gathered in early learning. SRGAP2C mice also displayed more structured behavior later in training and were, overall, better information channels than their WT counterparts. A computational model confirmed that SRGAP2C mice learning strategy increases representational capacity. Our results reveal that expression of human-specific gene SRGAP2C in cortical circuits is sufficient to increase the cognitive abilities of mice by optimizing the use of sensory information to guide action. The human-specific gene SRGAP2C might have contributed to the emergence of distinct functional cortical circuit features underlying our unique learning abilities and flexible decision-making.

papers.title: Resource-State Modulation of Prefrontal Value Processing during Earning-Spending Decision Making
papers.abstract: Money mediates earning and spending, and accumulated monetary holdings constitute both a basic form of wealth and an external resource state that shapes economic decisions. Unlike internal physiological states such as hunger or satiety, external resources persist outside the body, can be acquired or depleted through choice, and preserve access to future consumption. Although money and wealth are human constructs, balancing resource acquisition and consumption may rely on evolutionarily conserved neural computations. Here we investigated these computations using an earning-spending task, in which rhesus monkeys chose between earning virtual tokens and spending accumulated tokens for water, with holdings carrying across trials. As holdings varied, monkeys shifted between earning and spending choices. A state-dependent utility model explained this shift through opposing changes in the relative values of earning and spending. We recorded single-unit activities from the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Neuronal populations across all three regions represented current holdings, while ACC and OFC updated these representations after earning and spending outcomes. Crucially, resource state modulated value coding and reshaped the geometry of earning- and spending-value representations across all three regions. OFC exhibited a broader spectrum of signals spanning option value, chosen value, and good-based choice, whereas DLPFC representations were weighted more strongly toward action-based choice. Together, these findings identify distributed prefrontal mechanisms that represent, update, and use an external resource state to guide valuation and choice, extending neural accounts of state-dependent valuation beyond internal physiological conditions and suggesting an evolutionarily conserved foundation for balancing resource acquisition and consumption.

papers.title: Top-down prefrontal connectivity accompanies perceptual breakthrough after interocular suppression
papers.abstract: The role of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in the emergence of visual stimuli into conscious awareness remains contested. Additionally, whether top-down prefrontal connectivity is shaped by prior expectations during this process is not well understood. To address these questions, we applied dynamic causal modelling (DCM) to an EEG dataset during breaking continuous flash suppression (bCFS), which offers tight control over when a stimulus breaks into conscious perception. Our network comprised bilateral PFC, primary visual cortex, fusiform gyrus and motor cortex. Because perceptual breakthrough precedes behavioural report, we used a temporally resolved classifier to empirically define each participants moment of perceptual breakthrough (M = 1250ms, SD = 100ms). DCMs were then inverted over this time window up until each individuals breakthrough point. Parametric empirical Bayes revealed that top-down connectivity from the PFC to all regions was necessary to explain the observed neural dynamics (posterior probability [pp] > 0.99), though evidence that this top-down influence was modulated by expectation was inconclusive (pp = 0.74). Together, these findings suggest that top-down PFC connectivity accompanies perceptual breakthrough in bCFS, but it remains unclear whether this is modulated by expectation.

papers.title: Paternal transmission of the APPPS1 transgene is associated with increased amyloid pathology and a small Thy1.2-APP methylation difference
papers.abstract: Maternal transmission of the APP transgene lowers amyloid burden in 5xFAD mice. We examined whether APPPS1-21 shows a similar parent-of-origin association and whether Thy1.2 methylation contributes. F1 offspring inheriting the transgene from the mother had less A{beta}42, fewer plaques, less gliosis, and less human APP at intermediate ages. The A{beta}42 difference was not detected in the F2 cohort at 100 days. Non-transgenic off-spring of APPPS1 mothers did not differ in glial counts, and serum anti-A{beta} antibody levels were not higher at 40 days. In an exploratory methylation analysis of 32 brains, parent-of-origin-associated differences were sex-specific and enriched on chromosome X, not chromosome 2. The Thy1.2-APP cassette showed an approximately three-percentage-point paternal increase; the PSEN1 cassette did not. These findings establish an association with parental transmission but do not show that methylation causes the pathology differences. HIGHLIGHTSO_LIMaternal transmission is associated with lower amyloid pathology C_LIO_LIThe amyloid-beta 42 difference was not detected in the second generation C_LIO_LIAmyloid precursor protein cassette methylation is higher with paternal transmission C_LIO_LIThe methylation difference does not establish a causal mechanism C_LI IN BRIEFWe report lower amyloid pathology after F0 maternal APPPS1 transmission to F1. The A{beta}42 difference was not detected in the F2 cohort. The small Thy1.2-APP methylation difference does not establish a causal mechanism.

papers.title: Prethalamus integrates neocortical and hypothalamic input to promote courage
papers.abstract: Courage, the ability to act despite potential danger, is essential for adaptive behavior, yet the circuit mechanisms that balance caution and risk-taking under threat are not fully understood. Here we identify the ventral lateral geniculate nucleus (vLGN), an inhibitory prethalamic structure, as a key node in this process. High vLGN activity predicts courageous behavior, such as leaving a shelter to enter a potentially threatening environment, and optogenetic activation of vLGN neurons promotes risk-taking under diverse aversive conditions. Inputs to vLGN from retrosplenial cortex (RSC) and ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) modulate this behavior in opposing directions: RSC input promotes leaving safety, while VMH input suppresses it. These inputs target largely distinct vLGN populations that interact to integrate these opposing drives: a hypothalamic signal promoting defensive caution and a neocortical signal promoting action despite potential threat.

papers.title: Lifespan Remodeling of Cerebral Biomechanical Network Organization Reveals Coordinated Maturation and Aging-Related Convergence
papers.abstract: Brain biomechanical connectivity (BC) captures shared regional viscoelastic properties that may support functional interactions. Although functional and structural brain networks are well characterized, the systems-level organization of brain biomechanics remains unknown. Using in-vivo magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) and community detection, we established BC and its network organization across the mouse lifespan, spanning seven stages from early adolescence (4 weeks) to old age (72 weeks). BC was benchmarked against established functional and structural connectivity, revealing shared connectivity features. Biomechanical network organization showed increasing segregation during adolescence, peaking in late adolescence, followed by progressive reintegration with aging. Biomechanical network dynamics defined by the pace of age-related change showed coordinated maturation during adolescence, regionally differentiated trajectories throughout adulthood, and partial reconvergence in aging. These findings establish a lifespan framework for cerebral biomechanical connectivity in mice and reveal age-dependent systems-level network reorganization that may underlie critical windows of brain maturation, aging, and disease vulnerability.

papers.title: Closed-loop control of sensorimotor aperiodic neural dynamics can manipulate excitatory-inhibitory balance in humans
papers.abstract: A ubiquitous property of physical and biological systems is scale-free dynamics in which spectral power decreases as a function of frequency, showing a 1/f spectral slope. The 1/f slope of neural power spectra has been proposed as a marker of cortical excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, based on pharmacological experiments and computational models of synaptic activity in cortical networks. However, whether or not the spectral slope in the human population recordings, influenced by biophysical or experimental factors, can be utilized as an index of cortical E/I is debatable. Here, we show that this slope can be volitionally modulated and that its modulation is accompanied by changes in motor cortical activity reflecting E/I balance. To this end, we used a closed-loop paradigm in which real-time changes in the sensorimotor 1/f slope during neurofeedback trigger transcranial magnetic stimulation to probe intracortical circuits in the primary motor cortex. We found lower facilitatory effects in the steeper 1/f state than in both the flatter state and at rest, despite no significant between-state differences in 1/f-adjusted band power. These findings establish the physiological relevance of 1/f modulation with cortical states and support the contribution of intracortical E/I-related processes to the aperiodic dynamics.

papers.title: Evidence supporting resting-state power spectrum exponent as a non-invasive measure of neural-circuit excitation:inhibition balance in children with and without autism
papers.abstract: IntroductionAn ongoing neural circuit excitation (E) and inhibition (I) imbalance is thought to be a major contributor to clinical conditions such as autism, schizophrenia, and epilepsy. Current methods for directly measuring E:I dynamics require invasive procedures that are difficult to perform in non-human animals and nearly impossible in humans. A non-invasive measure of E:I balance is of great interest as a diagnostic as well as therapeutic marker, and as a means of studying relevant pathological and intervention mechanisms. Scientists have recently developed a computational model to show that, using resting-state (RS) MEG or EEG recordings, the E:I balance can be estimated from the power law exponent (slope) of the electrophysiological power spectrum. In their model, the RS power spectrum exponent is hypothesized to reflect the integration of synaptic currents in the brain, an index of E:I balance driven largely by excitatory (glutamate, Glu) and inhibitory (gamma-aminobutyric acid, GABA) neurotransmitter levels. Glu and GABA are the principal excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain, together shaping the balance between neural circuit excitation and inhibition. The present study shows that parietal-occipital neurochemistry as a predictor of the parietal-occipital RS exponent is driven by inhibitory neurotransmitter levels in typically developing (TD) children but not in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). MethodsMidline parietal-occipital RS power spectra (MEG) and Glu and GABA+ concentration (MRS) were obtained from 129 children (TD N = 84, ASD N = 45) 10.2 to 17.9 years old, with follow-up measures in a subset of the children providing 148 MEG and MRS datasets. Analyses focused on RS neural function and Glu and GABA+ concentration in parietal-occipital cortex. Resultst-tests showed no group differences between the parietal-occipital exponent, Glu, GABA+, or Glu/GABA+ ratio measures (ps > 0.21). In the full sample, older age was marginally associated with a lower exponent (p = 0.07), and older age associated with lower Glu concentration (p 0.05). There was no main effect of Glu or Glu x Group interaction with the exponent (ps > 0.14). Simple effect analyses of group interactions for GABA+ (p < 0.05) and ratio (p<0.05) showed a GABA+ and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.40) and a ratio and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.83). DiscussionThe brain chemistry and RS exponent associations suggest that a simple method for estimating E:I ratio reduces a major hurdle in understanding a currently difficult-to-measure, yet fundamental aspect of neural computation that has been proposed as central to clinical conditions such as ASD, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. Present findings indicate that the contribution of local brain chemistry to neural-circuit E:I balance differs for older children with and without ASD, with GABA inhibition presenting the more promising contributor to the E:I balance in TD children. Findings have the potential for high impact, including identifying neural markers for use in tracking treatment response.

papers.title: From cellular synaptic input profiles to population-level respiratory circuitry
papers.abstract: Breathing depends on coordinated activity among brainstem neurons. Their discharge patterns show when populations are active but do not specify the synaptic inputs that generate these patterns. Assuming that respiratory pattern generation involves a small number of interacting populations distinguished by discharge timing and excitatory or inhibitory output, we used synaptic conductances as readouts of their convergent activity. We reconstructed excitatory and inhibitory conductances from our previously described in situ rat brainstem-spinal cord recording archive (168 recordings, 150 neurons). We represented candidate presynaptic activity by five independently recorded population discharge patterns, assuming that phase-dependent inputs originated within these populations. We fitted each conductance time course as a nonnegative weighted sum of these patterns and tested whether candidate inputs could be omitted from the population mean, using variation across cells. Post-inspiratory inhibition was supported in all three inspiratory populations. Ramp-inspiratory neurons also showed augmenting-expiratory inhibition, and pre-inspiratory/inspiratory neurons showed augmenting-expiratory excitation. Excitation increased during the active phases of ramp-inspiratory and augmenting-expiratory neurons. Both expiratory populations showed inspiratory excitation alongside their prominent inspiratory inhibition. The inferred circuit retained major inhibitory interactions of the transection-based three-phase architecture and included additional excitatory inputs suggested by the earlier analysis. We distinguished some individual inspiratory discharge patterns but could not resolve other assignments. Source assignments depended on conductance reconstruction and how well the activity patterns represented presynaptic timing. These findings support excitatory interactions across populations with distinct discharge phases and suggest a contribution of late-expiratory excitation to recruitment of the next inspiration. Key pointsO_LIRespiratory discharge patterns show when neurons are active but not the synaptic interactions generating these patterns. Our recent work reconstructed previously unavailable excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs in respiratory neurons (Molkov et al., 2025). C_LIO_LIWe reconstructed inputs in a larger sample from the same archive and combined them with published population activity to identify candidate input sources for each receiving population and reconstruct a circuit. C_LIO_LIThe inferred circuit retained major inhibitory interactions of the three-phase architecture proposed to explain brainstem transection experiments. It included excitatory and inhibitory subpopulations with post-inspiratory and augmenting-expiratory discharge, with additional excitation during active and silent phases of receiving neurons. C_LIO_LISome inputs could be assigned to individual inspiratory discharge patterns, assuming representative activity patterns; overlapping activity left other assignments unresolved. C_LIO_LIExcitatory inputs link populations active in different phases. Rising late-expiratory excitation together with declining inhibition provides a candidate mechanism for recruitment of the next inspiration. C_LI

papers.title: Inferred interactions transform values into lattice-patterned choice attractors in orbitofrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Economic decisions require transforming option values into choices, a process involving the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), but the circuit mechanism remains unclear. We recorded OFC activity in monkeys performing a juice-choice task, fitted graphical Ising models to spike data, and simulated the inferred networks. Offer inputs shifted the networks toward attractor states favoring the choice representation supported by relative value. Targeted ablations revealed a core functional backbone for this transformation, linking offer-value and choice-tuned populations, alongside amplification by broader network interactions and complementary contributions from positive- and negative-encoding pathways. Mean interactions between tuning groups captured the average transformation, while finer interaction structure shaped its network-specific implementation. At single-neuron resolution, the transformation was expressed through a recurring response motif coupling activation and suppression in a spatial lattice. Together, these results reveal how inferred OFC interactions transform offer values into choice-selective attractor states and shape the lattice-patterned neuronal recruitment characterizing this transformation.

papers.title: Local sleep in wake is widespread across the rat cortex and tracks sleep need
papers.abstract: During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, cortical neurons alternate between ON periods of firing and OFF periods of silence, the latter accounting for the slow waves of the EEG. Converging evidence indicates that OFF periods can also occur locally during extended wake ("local sleep"), at a behavioral cost, but whether this phenomenon is ubiquitous across the cortex, whether some areas are more resilient than others, and whether it can also provide any benefit, remain open questions. Here we recorded from 11 cortical areas (and claustrum) in 15 rats using high-density Neuropixels probes and detected OFF periods with a novel method that captures spatially restricted and irregularly shaped events mischaracterized or missed by traditional methods. We found OFF periods during extended wake in every region tested, with no evidence that any area is spared. Over the course of sleep deprivation, OFF periods became more frequent, longer, larger, and quieter, and their features correlated with delta power on a per-event basis in both wake and NREM sleep, consistent with the notion that they reflect accumulating sleep need. The extent to which OFF periods overlapped across areas also increased across sleep deprivation. Finally, the rate of medium and large OFF periods during sleep deprivation was negatively correlated with their rebound in subsequent recovery sleep, consistent with the possibility that local sleep in wake partially discharges sleep need before the animal falls asleep. Statement of SignificanceProlonged wakefulness drives small groups of cortical neurons into brief sleep-like states even as the animal remains awake and behaving. This "local sleep" in wake is thought to underlie the errors and slowed responses of sleep deprivation, but how widespread it is, and whether it helps, remains unclear. Using high-density recordings across many cortical regions in the rat and a novel detection method sensitive to small, irregular events, we show that local sleep is not confined to a few vulnerable areas but occurs throughout the cortex, growing with accumulating sleep need. We also find that these neuronal lapses may begin to relieve that need before sleep takes over, suggesting that they may represent an early, piecemeal form of recovery.

papers.title: Forecasting Human Sleep Dynamics with a Latent-State Framework
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for health, and forecasting its evolution could clarify its temporal organization and guide intervention timing. We developed a representation-forecasting model using electroencephalography from 5,419 participants. From 30-minute histories, 10-minute forecasts achieved 90.71% four-class accuracy in the 10% of windows with lowest predicted risk and averaged 72.11% overall. Direction-specific encoder feature axes had spectral correlates. Forecast changes under fixed-strength perturbations along these axes can quantify window-specific sensitivity varying with observed transition destination and bout timing. Physiological validation linked greater simulated perturbation sensitivity to stronger observed sleep-state responses following acoustic stimulation and respiratory events. Clinical profiling linked older age and higher apnoea-hypopnoea index to stronger modeled Wake-directed and weaker N3-directed responses. These results demonstrated that sleep-state forecasting could quantify dynamics, prioritize candidate intervention windows, and help interpret post-intervention changes.

papers.title: One More Night: Investigating the Stability of Verbal Overnight Memory Consolidation and Sources of Variability
papers.abstract: Sleep-Dependent Memory Consolidation (SDMC) plays a vital role in facilitating the retention of newly learnt information. However, retesting in the literature is scarce and thus little is known regarding the daily stability of the SDMC process. The present study investigated whether overnight memory consolidation performance is stable (reflecting a trait) or variable (reflecting a state) across two nights using a novel word-pair smartphone application. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of subjective sleep quality and motivation on overnight consolidation performance, and whether these associations remained consistent across nights. Young healthy adults (N = 52) completed a validated word-pair task via a smartphone application over two nights and completed subjective sleep and motivation questionnaires. Results indicated overnight consolidation performance was not stable across nights, despite same-day and next-day recall exhibiting significant stability. Subjective sleep and motivation scores were not associated with performance, although these associations remained consistent across nights. However, worse PSQI scores were associated with lower next-day recall. After considering semantically related and unrelated word-pairs, both same-day and next-day recall performance exhibited significant stability for unrelated word-pairs only. These findings question the reliance on single-night SDMC protocols, and future research should examine modifiable factors that underlie SDMC variability across nights.

papers.title: Dynamic Weight Signatures as a Novel Biomarker of Motor Dysfunction in Mouse Models
papers.abstract: Motor dysfunction is typically assessed through clinical examination and manual scoring, with gait analysis and accelerometry providing objective measures of subtle abnormalities. The observable 4-6 Hz resting tremor of Parkinsons disease highlights the importance of capturing motor fluctuations at relevant timescales. Using a high-precision industrial weighing module, we tested whether high-frequency weight recordings of freely moving mice could provide a simple, noninvasive means of detecting disease-associated motor abnormalities. Aging MitoPark mice spend more time in non-ambulatory states and exhibit less stable locomotion than healthy controls; however, bradykinesia and shaking can be mitigated by intraperitoneal levodopa. Here we demonstrate that irregular motor activity and tremor-like movements are quantifiable via weight frequency analyses, which permit detection of early symptoms and post-levodopa motor control restoration. This non-invasive approach is less data-intensive than video-based analyses, adaptable for home-cage monitoring, and potentially translatable for clinical or home use for detection of subclinical motor dysfunction.

papers.title: Behaviorally driven increased glutamatergic activity from lateral entorhinal cortex to hippocampus supports object and spatial memory recall
papers.abstract: Interactions between the entorhinal cortex (EC) and hippocampal area CA1 are vital for episodic memory formation, but their role in recall is less clear. Canonically, spatial processing -- the "where" of an experience -- is attributed to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), whereas the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) processes the "what": non-spatial sensory cues and objects. Though these inputs are anatomically segregated in CA1, multimodal memory processing requires integrating spatial and contextual information, and recent work suggests greater MEC-LEC crosstalk than previously thought. Global LEC silencing via lesions, or combined suppression of glutamatergic and GABAergic LEC neurons, impairs associational goal-oriented learning and multi-object-cued encoding. However, the role of LEC glutamatergic projections specifically to CA1 during recall in freely moving spatial behaviors, and their contribution to synaptic plasticity, remains unclear. We used fiber photometry to record LEC axonal calcium dynamics in CA1 during novel object recognition and Barnes maze tasks, and ex vivo electrophysiology with LEC optogenetic activation. LEC activity increased during recall in both tasks, especially as animals learned spatial cues, peaking at late training stages of the Barnes maze. Local chemogenetic silencing of LEC inputs in CA1 after learning impaired recall. Ex vivo, temporally precise optogenetic activation of LEC input paired with CA3 intrahippocampal inputs was sufficient to induce long-term potentiation of both pathways in CA1 pyramidal neurons. These results suggest that LEC glutamatergic input to CA1 is dynamically modulated by experience to support recall during both object recognition and spatial navigation, with a functional role in synaptic plasticity.

papers.title: An expanded GRAB sensor palette for multiplexed imaging of purinergic dynamics in vivo
papers.abstract: Extracellular ATP and adenosine operate as tightly coupled purinergic signals, yet tracking both molecules simultaneously in vivo has been limited by the performance and spectral range of existing sensors. We describe an expanded set of genetically encoded GPCR-Activation-Based (GRAB) sensors for ATP and adenosine that together support multiplexed imaging of purinergic signaling in the intact brain. Systematic optimization of receptor scaffolds, membrane trafficking, and fluorophore coupling yielded next-generation green sensors (Ado2h, Ado2m, ATP2h, ATP2l) and spectrally separated red variants (rAdo1h, rATP1h), each combining high ligand specificity, genetically targetable expression, sub-second kinetics, and minimal engagement of endogenous GPCR pathways. This combination allows minimally invasive, dual-color imaging of purinergic activity in vivo. Using multiplexed fiber photometry and two-photon imaging, we tracked ATP and adenosine concurrently across several behavioral and pathological settings. ATP release preceded extracellular adenosine accumulation during sleep-wake transitions and neuronal activation, a pattern consistent with extracellular ATP hydrolysis as a substantial contributor to in vivo adenosine signaling. During epileptic seizures, paired imaging of extracellular ATP with extracellular adenosine, and of extracellular with intracellular adenosine, indicated distinct spatiotemporal dynamics across cellular compartments. This expanded sensor set offers a platform for multiplexed purinergic imaging and for probing ATP-adenosine coupling across physiological and pathological brain states.

papers.title: Ion-channel transcript loss and variable firing in SCA1 Purkinje cells: a modelling test
papers.abstract: In spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), Purkinje cells fire with more variable interspike intervals before they degenerate, and reduced ion-channel expression is a proposed cause. We asked whether their channel transcript changes, applied as conductance changes, could produce this firing. We analysed public single-nucleus RNA-seq from male and female Atxn1 154Q/2Q knock-in and wild-type mice (24 discovery mice, 5-30 weeks; six held-out, 12 weeks). Knock-in Purkinje nuclei showed a reproducible transcriptional shift from 5 weeks. Transcripts of five channels, Kv3.3, BK, Kv4.3, Cav2.1 and Cav3.1, were reduced by 12 weeks (28-41 % at 18 weeks) and also lower, though not significantly for any single transcript, in ATXN1[82Q] Purkinje nuclei. We scaled the five conductances by these ratios in a published Purkinje cell model (130 parameter sets). The simulated neurons fired at 1.9 times the wild-type rate, outside the range recorded in knock-in Purkinje cells, and at 1.14 times in a second model. Scaling only Kv3.3, BK, Kv4.3 and Cav3.1, with Cav2.1 left at its wild-type value, brought both models close to the wild-type rate. With BK and Cav3.1 set from published staining, the afterhyperpolarization and depolarization-block threshold moved towards knock-in values, but by less. Dividing the five transcript ratios by the smaller knock-in membrane area (0.80 of wild type) also brought the median firing rate into the recorded range. Among versions whose median firing rate was in the recorded range, the median over parameter sets of the KI/WT ratio of the interspike-interval coefficient of variation was at most 1.57, whereas the recorded ratios of the group means were 1.8 and 2.9. In some versions, pauses in a few simulated neurons raised the ratio of the mean coefficients of variation. In these models, transcript changes alone did not reproduce the firing. Measuring spontaneous firing, Cav2.1 current density and membrane capacitance in the same knock-in and wild-type Purkinje cells, matched for age and lobule, would show whether Cav2.1 current falls less than its transcript, whether the cells are smaller, or both. Significance StatementIn spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), Purkinje cells fire with more variable interspike intervals before they degenerate. Five ion-channel transcripts are lower in SCA1 knock-in Purkinje cells and, though not significantly for any single transcript, in a second SCA1 model. We asked whether these lower transcripts, taken as smaller conductances, explain the firing. In a Purkinje cell model, reducing all five conductances made the simulated neurons fire almost twice as fast as wild type, unlike knock-in Purkinje cells. Keeping Cav2.1 at its wild-type value, or correcting for the smaller knock-in membrane, brought the median firing rate close to that of knock-in cells, but the median increase in the variability of the interspike interval stayed below the recorded increase. Measuring spontaneous firing, Cav2.1 current density and membrane capacitance in the same knock-in and wild-type Purkinje cells, matched for age and lobule, would show whether Cav2.1 current falls less than its transcript, whether the cells are smaller, or both.

papers.title: Cross-Stream Self-Supervised Learning Inspired by Feature-Biased Visual Processing in the Brain
papers.abstract: Humans and other animals develop rich visual representations without explicit object-category labels. Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a computational framework for studying how such representations emerge from visual experience. Many contrastive SSL models, such as SimCLR, learn by being robust to augmented views of the same image, which may fail to preserve visual attributes such as color and orientation. Inspired by feature-specific visual processing streams in the brain, we propose BioCLR, an SSL framework that uses color- and orientation-biased networks to guide representation learning. We combine Bio-CLR with SimCLR into a BioCLR hybrid model, pretrain it on ImageNet-100, and evaluate it on this dataset and four transfer datasets. In frozen linear evaluation, the BioCLR hybrid outperforms SimCLR across all datasets and mitigates negative transfer on a handwritten-character dataset. In limited-label fine-tuning, it outperforms SimCLR in most transfer conditions. Compared with the AugSelf and RotNet hybrids, which incorporate color and orientation information into SimCLR in other ways, the BioCLR hybrid shows the best overall performance, particularly in limited-label fine-tuning. Ablation analyses suggest that orientation guidance helps more than color guidance on these datasets, and that combining both generally improves frozen linear evaluation performance. Together, these findings suggest that incorporating feature-specific information into SSL can improve representation quality and model adaptability, and that the learning mechanism used to incorporate this information matters. For neuroscience, these results suggest that specialized visual streams in the brain may provide learning signals that guide visual representation learning without explicit supervision. For machine learning, they imply that principles of feature-biased processing in visual cortex may improve SSL.

papers.title: Dynamic remodeling of hybrid BBB-fenestrated capillaries in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus
papers.abstract: The hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (Arc) is a central regulator of metabolism. We show that capillaries with sparse fenestrae enable direct and rapid hormone transport into the Arc. Arc fenestrae are virtually absent during pregnancy and obesity, but reform postpartum and upon weight-loss. Fenestrated Arc endothelial cells display a unique hybrid BBB-permeable structural and molecular phenotype, which can be regulated by Wnt signaling. The Arc endothelium exhibits functional plasticity that may affect hypothalamic sensing of systemic metabolic signals.

papers.title: Robustness of a connectome model of the fly walking rhythm generator to modelling choices
papers.abstract: Connectome-constrained models are increasingly used to attribute behaviour to wiring, but their conclusions rest on modelling choices that the connectome does not fix. We independently replicated the rate model of the Drosophila nerve cord in which descending neuron DNg100 drives a walking rhythm generator (Pugliese et al., 2026), and asked which of its conclusions survive defensible alternatives to eleven such choices. Changed one at a time, 19 of 20 alternatives left the rhythm intact, including transfer of the wiring to a second connectome. Changed jointly, the rhythm survived in only 20 of 48 model variants when the descending drive was set by rules that do not look at the rhythm. A post hoc sweep of the drive separated two causes. In 12 of the 28 failures a rhythm existed at another drive, in 11 of them a higher one: the published drive lies at the lower edge of the rhythmic range. The other failures concentrated where larger networks met two- or threefold heterogeneity of intrinsic parameters, an interaction that one-at-a-time tests cannot show. In the 31 variants with a rhythm at a common drive of the sweep, the two excitatory interneurons remained necessary (30 of 31) and the inhibitory interneuron dispensable (29 of 31). The rhythm stayed rare among degree-preserving rewired networks when their drive was swept as well, and left-right coupling in the model was weak. The operating point is a modelling choice in its own right, and what a connectome model "produces" should be reported across it.

papers.title: Global weight-Ranked cluster-grOWing (GROW): A Cluster-Growing Framework for Robust Functional Coordinate Network Mapping
papers.abstract: Coordinate Network Mapping (CNM) has become an important approach for translating scattered neuroimaging findings into circuit-level models of brain disorders such as Alzheimers disease (AD). But conventional CNM uses fixed-radius spheres and pools heterogeneous studies without accounting for confounders. We developed Global weight-Ranked cluster-grOWing (GROW), which reconstructs clusters behind reported peaks using cluster information and a reference statistical weight map, without original imaging data. We analyzed data from 521 participants and 69 published studies (82 experiments, 5,555 participants). GROW-CNM was compared with fixed-radius CNM (Fixed-CNM) in spatial fidelity, cross-study convergence, sampling stability, and sensitivity to confounders. At study level, Fixed-CNM corresponded poorly with the reference atrophy-derived functional network in AD (Spearman r = -0.24, overlap = 1.61%), and radius changes did not improve fidelity. In contrast, GROW-CNM recovered cluster morphology and generated maps closer to the reference network (r [≥] 0.85, overlap [≥] 87.30%). GROW-CNM also showed greater cross-study convergence (median peak probability, 0.99 vs. 0.67; z = 27.42, p < 0.001) and was robust to threshold/resampling (z = -169.84, p < 0.001). Fixed-CNM was associated with systematic factors; GROW-CNM was more sensitive to demographic confounders (p < 0.05, TFCE-FWE correction). Systematic confounding was attenuated by GROW-CNM; Fixed-CNM remained susceptible in core regions (p < 0.001). These findings indicate cross-study heterogeneity in coordinate-based AD network maps reflects seed definition and study-level confounders, not biology alone. Combining GROW-based seed reconstruction with confounder-adjusted population modeling may provide a robust framework for mapping disease-related brain networks and prioritizing candidate neuromodulation targets.

papers.title: A Deep Learning Model for Quantifying and Mapping Human Spiral Ganglion Neurons (SGNs): The SGN Base Model
papers.abstract: IntroductionSpiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) transmit auditory information and are a histological marker that have been quantified for decades to study various hearing loss pathologies in human temporal bone (hTB) specimens. Historically, quantification of SGNs has been labor-intensive and subject to manual bias and error. With the advent of digital microscopy, this study introduces and assesses the accuracy of a deep learning model for SGN quantification, providing an efficient approach that enables in-depth analysis of SGN distribution through three-dimensional frequency mapping. MethodsDigitized mid-modiolar slides from six hTBs from the Mass Eye and Ear Otopathology Laboratory Collection, representing a range of ages, post-mortem times, and diagnoses, were selected to train a computer vision model. Using Dragonfly 2024.1, the nucleus and cytoplasm of each SGN were manually segmented against background and used as the training corpus. The model was systemically evaluated in eighteen new cases to assess its accuracy across diverse histopathological presentations. For the specimen with the lowest performance, five small regions were manually annotated to augment the training dataset to evaluate the adaptability of the model. Next, the model was applied to every available slide that includes Rosenthals canal for a single case to assess model performance throughout the entire cochlea. Model performance was evaluated by comparing model SGN counts with counts by an experienced investigator, classifying each model prediction as a true positive, false positive, or false negative. Using coordinates output by the model, three-dimensional reconstructions were generated to analyze model performance from base to apex. ResultsA U-Net convolutional neural network was developed with an average Dice coefficient of 0.91. Across eighteen cases representing diverse SGN morphologies and densities, the model achieved an F1-score of 0.91. For the case with the lowest performance, fine-tuning the model by adding additional training data from the same case improved the r2 value from 0.919 to 0.996. When applied to all available slides from a single case, the model achieved an F1-score of 0.96 across the entire cochlea. ConclusionWe present the pretrained SGN Base Model: an approach for quantifying SGNs in hTB specimens that improves efficiency while maintaining high accuracy in comparison to manual quantification. The model performs robustly throughout the cochlea and is adaptable to a diverse range of archival hTB specimens with variable SGN densities and morphologies. Model-generated spatial coordinates for each SGN enable three-dimensional analysis and detailed mapping of SGN density from base to apex.

papers.title: Olfactory-Visual Integration Facilitates Scene Perception through Modulation of the Parahippocampal Place Area
papers.abstract: Visual scenes anchor our experience of the world, yet the places in which scenes unfold are defined not only by what we see but also by what we smell. Whether and how odors contribute to the neural representation of visual scenes remains poorly understood. Here we asked whether a semantically congruent odor facilitates scene perception and identified the neural mechanisms supporting this facilitation. In two behavioral experiments, participants judged whether briefly presented, masked images depicted intact or scrambled scenes while continuously smelling an odor. A congruent odor lowered the exposure duration needed for accurate scene detection, and a placebo experiment, in which participants merely believed they were smelling an odor, failed to reproduce this benefit, indicating that the facilitation depends on actual sensory input rather than semantic priming. In an fMRI experiment, congruent odors enhanced responses and sharpened category-level scene representations in the parahippocampal place area (PPA), with the congruency-driven enhancement localized to the same anterior subregion that encoded scene identity. A conjunction analysis revealed superadditive responses to congruent odor-scene pairs in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and hippocampus, and psychophysiological interaction analyses showed that congruent stimulation strengthened functional coupling among the OFC, PPA, and piriform cortex. Notably, the piriform cortex decoded visual scene identity after congruent odor-scene pairing, suggesting that odor-scene binding extends scene representations into primary olfactory cortex. Together, these findings identify the PPA as a site where olfactory signals refine the neural code for visual scenes and reveal an OFC-coordinated piriform-OFC-PPA network through which smell shapes our sense of place.

papers.title: Sex-Related Associations Between Precuneus Volume and Subjective-Objective Memory Discrepancy in Amyloid-Positive Individuals
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTIONThe precuneus, a metamemory-related parietal region with sex-specific vulnerability in Alzheimers disease (AD), may contribute to reduced insight of memory deficit. We investigated whether precuneus structural integrity explained sex differences in subjective-objective memory discrepancy. METHODSPrecuneus volumes, as well as three other control regions, were acquired in 350 A{beta}+ and 310 A{beta}-participants from the ADNI dataset to quantify within-individual changes in subjective-objective memory discrepancy across AD progression. RESULTSA{beta}+ participants exhibited steeper objective memory decline ({beta} = -0.446, p < 0.001) despite stable subjective complaints ({beta} = -0.027, p = 0.587), resulting in a widening subjective-objective memory discrepancy ({beta} = 0.317, p < 0.001). In this group, only precuneus atrophy showed a sex-dependent association with discrepancy ({beta} = 0.508, p = 0.002), a finding absent in the A{beta}- group or other brain regions. DISCUSSIONThe precuneus represents a neuroanatomical substrate associated with sex-related differences in metacognitive vulnerability in A{beta}+ individuals.
